title: When It All Comes Apart
subtitle: A five-session study on faith deconstruction, handled pastorally, for the person taking an inherited faith apart to see what is actually true.
summary:
This study is for the person pulling a faith apart piece by piece, for the friends and pastors who love them and do not know what to say, and for small groups willing to sit with hard questions without panicking. It walks slowly through five movements, on what you are actually taking apart when you say you are deconstructing, on whether doubt is a sin and the Bible's long line of honest doubters, on the wounds that come when the church itself is the reason, on rebuilding on rock rather than on the rubble of what you tore down, and on a faith small enough to be true and strong enough to hold weight. It is built to be run by a busy volunteer with no preparation. Every question carries the answer behind it, every silence has a backup, and every session ends in prayer rather than a verdict.

This is not a study that tries to talk anyone out of their questions, and the leader must never let it become that. Deconstruction is not a betrayal and it is not a fad. It is what an honest person does when the answers they were handed stop carrying weight. Many people taking their faith apart are not leaving Jesus. They are leaving a version of him somebody sold them, and the difference between those two departures is the whole question this study exists to help people see. Some of what gets torn down deserves to come down, the cultural baggage, the borrowed certainty, the politics dressed as the gospel. Some of what gets torn down is the load-bearing wall, and the cost of pulling it out only shows up later. The study holds both without flinching, and it refuses to make faithful sifting sound like abandonment or to make abandonment sound like courage. Most of all it implicates the writer and the leader. Bell does not stand outside this. He is a pastor, and pastors like him did the bundling, wrapping God and the institution and the politics into one package and handing it over as though it were all the same thing. He has watched people leave over what the church did and called it their unbelief. He has the questions too. So will you.
audience: Those deconstructing, their friends and pastors, and small groups

sessions.title: What You Are Actually Taking Apart
sessions.aim: To stop the panic on both sides and do the first honest work, which is not deciding but sorting, separating the gospel from the cultural baggage it arrived wrapped in, so that whatever a person decides, they decide about the real thing.
sessions.summary: A man told Bell he was done with the whole thing, done with God, and when Bell asked him what exactly he was done with, the list that came out was a list of people and politics and one furious memory of a deacon, and God was barely in it. He was not done with God. He was done with a package, and somebody had taught him the package was God. The first question is not whether to keep the faith or leave it. It is what you are actually holding when you say faith, because for most of us it arrived as one bundle, the doctrine and the institution and the people and God himself, all handed over together as if they were the same thing. Bell takes the strong form of two answers that want to silence each other. The first says deconstruction is just rebellion dressed up, a person wanting to sin who needs a respectable reason, and it is right that some deconstruction is exactly that, a search for permission. The second says the inherited faith was all baggage, nothing but control and culture, and that the honest move is to torch it whole, and it is right that a great deal of what we were handed really was baggage and deserves the fire. Bell will not let either win. Not all questioning is rebellion, which refutes the first, and not all of the inherited faith is baggage, which refutes the second. The work is to tell the gospel from the wrapping, and pastors like Bell are the ones who taped them together in the first place. So the study does not begin with a verdict. It begins with a sorting, slow and unhurried, because nobody can decide honestly about a thing they have not yet separated from everything it came bundled with.

keyScripture.why: Paul tells the church to test everything and hold fast to what is good, which is not a command to keep everything and not a permission to discard everything, but an instruction to sift, to put the inherited thing under examination and keep only what survives the testing.

discussion.q: When you say you are losing your faith, or doubting it, or taking it apart, which faith do you actually mean, and who first taught it to you?
discussion.behind: Surface the bundle before anything gets decided. Most people in the room have never separated the four things, God, the doctrine, the institution, and the people, because they were handed as one package. The aim is not to settle anything yet but to expose how much of what feels like losing God is really losing the wrapping. Land it on honesty, not consensus. Go first if the room is slow.

discussion.q: Bell says pastors like him taped the package together, wrapping God and the politics and the institution into one thing and calling it all the gospel. Where can you feel that taping in your own inherited faith?
discussion.behind: Move the room off the instinct to defend the church or to attack it. The point is recognition, that the bundling was done to us, often by people who meant well, and that feeling everything fall at once is the result of the taping, not proof that everything is equally false. Help them see the bundle so they can begin to untie it.

discussion.q: Bell takes the strong form of the view that deconstruction is just rebellion looking for permission to sin. What is true in that, and what does it become when it is aimed at every person with a real question?
discussion.behind: Protect the even-handedness from the start. Some deconstruction really is a search for permission, and the room should not leave thinking every question is pure. But make sure they also see what the accusation becomes when a pastor swings it at someone whose faith genuinely broke on a real wound or a real contradiction. The error is not naming rebellion. It is using the word to dodge a legitimate question.

discussion.q: Bell takes the other strong form too, that the inherited faith was all baggage and the honest move is to burn it whole. What is true there, and what does that view miss?
discussion.behind: Hold the second half just as honestly. A great deal of what we were handed was baggage, and saying so is not bitterness. The miss is the assumption that because some of it was wrapping, all of it was, which throws out the gospel with the politics. Help the room feel that wholesale exit is as unexamined as wholesale defense.

discussion.q: Bell admits he has watched people leave over what the church did to them and quietly filed it under their unbelief, which let him off the hook. Where have you mislabeled someone's leaving, or your own, to make it easier to live with?
discussion.behind: Move from diagnosis to self-implication. You are not hunting for confession to shame anyone. You want each person, the leader included, inside the honesty, because nobody sorts the bundle well while defending their own innocence. Go first, and name your own mislabeling out loud.

objections.objection: Deconstruction is just rebellion with better branding. People want to sin, or want to be approved of by people who do, and they need a respectable reason to walk away, so they call their wandering a search for truth.
objections.response: Sit with the half that is true, because Bell grants it. Some deconstruction really is a search for permission, the heart looking for an honest-sounding door out of a claim it has already decided to leave, and pretending that never happens would itself be a lie. Then make the distinction with care. The same suspicion, swung as a club, becomes a way for the church to avoid every legitimate question by accusing the questioner of bad motives. A person whose faith broke on a contradiction nobody would answer, or on a pastor who covered for an abuser, is not rebelling. They are responding honestly to something real. To call that rebellion is not discernment. It is a refusal to look at what the church did, and it drives the wounded straight out the door you accused them of wanting.

objections.objection: If you are questioning the faith at all, you never really had it. Real faith does not doubt. The fact that you are taking it apart proves it was never genuine in the first place.
objections.response: Grant the grain of truth, that some faith is shallow and built on things that were always going to crack, and that a crisis can reveal a foundation was never there. Then press the other edge, because the claim collapses under the Bible itself. The psalmist asks why God has forgotten him. John the Baptist, from prison, sends to ask whether Jesus is even the one. Thomas refuses to believe without seeing. These are not the rebels of Scripture. They are its heroes, and their faith was real precisely because it was honest enough to ask. To say questioning proves you never believed is to make doubters of nearly every saint in the book. Faith is not the absence of questions. It is what you do with them, and where you take them.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What is the one thing you say you have lost faith in that, if you are honest, you have never actually examined on its own, apart from everything it came bundled with?
sessions.practice: This week, each day write one sentence naming one specific thing you no longer believe or are no longer sure of. Then mark it with a single word, doctrine, institution, people, or God. Just the sorting. No verdicts, no deciding, no arguing yourself into or out of anything. At the end of the week, look at the list and notice which column is heaviest, and sit with what that tells you.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, we were handed a package and told it was all you, and now that it is coming apart we cannot tell what is you and what was only the wrapping. Forgive the church for the taping, and forgive us where we have torched the whole thing rather than do the slow work of sorting, and where we have defended the whole thing rather than admit some of it deserved to fall. Give us the courage to test everything and the patience to hold fast to what is good. We are not asking you to make the questions go away. We are asking you to be in the room while we ask them. Amen.
reflection: When everything felt like it was falling at once, was it really all falling, or was it the bundle coming apart, and have I ever tried to tell the pieces apart?
Where have I called something God when it was really the institution, or the politics, or the people who taught me, and what changes if I name it correctly?
Am I more tempted to defend the whole package or to burn it whole, and what is each of those temptations protecting me from having to examine?
sessions.teaching: Start where Bell starts, with a man across a table who said he was done with the whole thing, done with God. Bell asked him a simple question. Done with what, exactly. And the list that came out was a list of people. A father who quoted Scripture and hit his children. A church that closed ranks around a man everyone knew. A politics preached from the pulpit as though it were the fourth person of the Trinity. A deacon, one furious memory of a deacon, that the man could not get past. And God, the actual God, was barely in the list at all. He was not done with God. He was done with a package, and somewhere along the way somebody had taught him the package was God. So we do not begin where everyone wants to begin, with should you keep the faith or leave it, because that question cannot even be answered yet. We begin with the harder and more honest one. What are you actually holding when you say the word faith. Because for almost all of us it did not arrive as a single clean thing. It arrived as a bundle. The doctrine and the institution and the people and God himself, all wrapped together and handed over as though they were one object, so that to pull on any thread is to feel the whole thing come loose. And here I have to tell you who did the wrapping, because it was not strangers. It was pastors. It was people like me. We bundled God and the building and the voting guide and the cultural preferences of our particular tribe, and we taped them together and called the whole package the gospel, and we handed it to you that way. So when the tape starts to give, everything feels like it is falling at once. But it is not. The feeling is the bundling, not the truth. Take the two answers that want to shout each other down, and take them at full strength. The first says deconstruction is just rebellion with better branding, a person who wants to sin, or wants the approval of people who do, hunting for a respectable reason to leave. And it is not entirely wrong. Some deconstruction is exactly that, the heart looking for an honest-sounding door out of a claim it has already decided to walk away from, and pretending that never happens would be its own dishonesty. The second answer says the inherited faith was all baggage, nothing but control and culture and the politics of dead men, and that the only honest move is to torch it whole. And this answer is not wrong either. An enormous amount of what we were handed really was baggage. The certainty we did not own. The fear dressed as holiness. The party loyalty smuggled in beside the cross. A great deal of it deserves the fire. Now watch what happens when you refuse to let either answer take the whole field. Not all questioning is rebellion, which destroys the first position, because the Bible's own heroes questioned, and a faith that cannot survive a question was never standing on much. But not all of the inherited faith is baggage, which destroys the second, because tangled up in the wrapping is the actual gospel, the thing that was true even when the people teaching it were not, and to burn it whole is to lose the one part worth keeping along with all the parts worth losing. So here is the verdict, and the leader must hold it cleanly all the way through. The work in front of you is not deciding. It is sorting. It is the slow, unglamorous labor of telling the gospel from the wrapping it came in, of putting each piece down on the table and asking what it actually is, doctrine or institution or people or God. Some of what you are taking apart should come apart, and you can let it fall without guilt. Some of it is load-bearing, and the cost of pulling it out will not show up until later. And almost none of it can be judged honestly while it is still taped to everything else. And I have to stand inside this, because I have done the mislabeling too. I have watched people leave over a real wound the church gave them, and I have quietly filed their leaving under unbelief, because unbelief was a category that let me off the hook and made their exit their fault instead of partly ours. That was cowardice wearing the costume of discernment. The truth names the writer before it names the reader. So we will not rush to a verdict in this room. We will start where honesty actually starts, with the sorting, laying the pieces out one at a time, because no one has ever decided well about a thing they have not yet separated from everything it arrived bundled with. Test everything, Paul says. Hold fast to what is good. That is not keep it all, and it is not burn it all. It is sift. And the sifting is where we begin.

scriptureStudy.note: Test everything, hold fast to what is good. Paul does not tell the church to accept everything handed to them or to reject it, he tells them to examine it and keep what survives, which is the whole posture of faithful sorting.

The Bereans are called noble because they searched the Scriptures daily to see whether what Paul preached was true. Examining the teaching, even an apostle's, is praised here, not punished. Questioning was a mark of seriousness, not rebellion.

I believe, help my unbelief. The father brings Jesus a faith that is real and partial at the same time, and Jesus does not turn him away for the unbelief mixed in. Honest, divided faith is still welcomed.

Jesus rebukes the religious leaders for tithing their spices while neglecting justice and mercy and faithfulness, the weightier matters. He himself sorts the inherited religion, distinguishing the load-bearing from the baggage, which is exactly the work the study calls for.

These people honor me with their lips while their hearts are far from me, and their fear of me is a commandment taught by men. God names the difference between himself and the human traditions wrapped around him, the very bundling this session is about.

Paul says he was advanced in Judaism beyond his peers, zealous for the traditions of his fathers, and that zeal aimed him straight at persecuting the church. Inherited religious certainty is no proof of being right. Even sincerity can be pointed in the wrong direction.

Can anything good come out of Nazareth, Nathanael asks, and Philip answers come and see. The honest question is not rebuked. It is met with an invitation to look at the real thing rather than the assumption about it.

sessions.goingDeeper: Take up the long Christian distinction between the gospel itself and the cultural forms it has worn, because the bundling this session names is not new, it is one of the oldest problems in the church. From the very first generation the question was whether a Gentile had to become a cultural Jew in order to follow a Jewish Messiah, and the Jerusalem council in Acts 15 ruled that the wrapping was not the gospel, that circumcision and the dietary law were not the thing itself. The same fight has recurred in every age, when the faith arrived in a new place fused to the customs of the missionaries who carried it, so that converts were handed European dress and European politics alongside the cross and told it was all one package. Set this beside the modern situation, in which a particular national identity and a particular partisan loyalty have been so thoroughly fused with Christianity in some quarters that to question the politics feels, to the person raised in it, like questioning God. A serious group should weigh how the church has repeatedly mistaken its own cultural skin for its bones, and how the work of every reforming generation has been to tell the difference, to ask which commitments are the faith once delivered to the saints and which are merely the preferences of the people who happened to hand it on. The discipline this whole study requires begins here, in the refusal to treat the wrapping as the gift, and the equal refusal to throw out the gift because it came wrapped.
sessions.caseStudy: A woman in her thirties came to Bell and said she was deconstructing, and she said it the way a person confesses a diagnosis, braced for the lecture. He asked her to tell him the first thing that cracked. It was not a doctrine. It was a youth pastor, fifteen years earlier, who had told her that her questions about hell were a door the devil was using, and that good girls did not ask them. She had buried the question and the shame together, and they had sat there fermenting for fifteen years, and now the whole structure was coming down at once, the politics she had been handed and the certainty and the God who, in her mind, agreed with the youth pastor. Bell did not argue any of it. He took out a piece of paper and drew four columns, doctrine, institution, people, God, and he asked her to put the youth pastor somewhere. She put him under people. Then the hell question. She hesitated, and put it under doctrine, and said, quietly, that she had never once examined it on its own, only fled it. And God. She looked at the empty fourth column for a long time and said she did not actually know what she believed about God, because she had never met him apart from the people who claimed to speak for him. That was the whole session, right there, in the empty column. She had spent fifteen years sure she was losing God, and she had never once been alone in a room with him to find out. The sorting did not solve anything that night. But it was the first time the falling had stopped feeling like one undifferentiated avalanche and started feeling like a pile of separate things, some of which she could set down without guilt, and one of which, the fourth column, she had never yet picked up.

memoryVerse.text: Test everything, and hold fast to what is good.

sessions.title: Is Doubt a Sin
sessions.aim: To answer the question plainly, that honest doubt is not a sin, and to put the Bible's long line of doubters in front of the room, so that no one in the middle of real questions believes their questioning has already put them outside the door.
sessions.summary: Somebody, somewhere, taught most of us that doubt is the opposite of faith, that to question is to fail, and so the person in the middle of real questions carries a second weight on top of the first, the fear that the doubting itself is a sin that has already condemned them. The first question is whether that is even true. Bell answers it plainly. No. And then he proves it from the book the accusers claim to be defending. Bell takes the strong form of the worried believer who says doubt must be dangerous, because Scripture does warn against being double-minded and tossed like a wave, and that warning is real. He grants it. But then he opens the Bible and the doubters are everywhere, and they are not the villains. The psalmist demands to know how long God will hide his face. Job argues with God for chapters and is the one God vindicates against the friends who defended him. John the Baptist, the greatest born of women by Jesus's own word, sends from prison to ask whether Jesus is even the one he announced. Thomas refuses to believe without putting his hand in the wounds, and Jesus does not curse him, he shows up and offers the wounds. The verdict is that the Bible does not treat honest doubt as the enemy of faith. It treats it as something faith does on its way through. There is a kind of doubt that is corrosive, the doubt that refuses every answer and loves the question more than the truth, and Bell names it. But the doubt that asks because it wants to know, the doubt that takes its questions to God rather than away from him, is not the opposite of faith. It is faith being honest. And the difference between the two is not whether you doubt. It is which direction you carry the doubt.

keyScripture.why: Have mercy on those who doubt, Jude writes, placing the doubter not in the category of the rebel to be expelled but in the category of the one to be treated with mercy, which is the entire posture the church owes the questioning and so rarely gives.

discussion.q: Before tonight, what did you privately believe about doubt, that it was normal, or that it was a failure you were supposed to hide and pray away?
discussion.behind: Surface the default before correcting it. Many in the room carry an unexamined verdict that their doubting is itself a sin, and that verdict adds shame to an already heavy load. The aim is to expose the assumption so the rest of the session can answer it. Land on honesty, not on quick reassurance. Go first if the room is slow.

discussion.q: The Bible is full of doubters, the psalmist, Job, John the Baptist, Thomas, and they are not its villains. Why do you think the church so often teaches the opposite, that doubt is the enemy of faith?
discussion.behind: Move the room to notice the gap between what Scripture does with doubters and what the church does with them. The aim is not to bash the church but to see that the fear of doubt is often more cultural than biblical, a control mechanism rather than a faithful reading. Let them sit in the contrast.

discussion.q: Bell grants there is a corrosive kind of doubt, the doubt that loves the question more than the truth and refuses every answer. How would you tell that apart from honest doubt in your own heart?
discussion.behind: This is the hinge. Do not let the room conclude all doubt is automatically healthy, because Bell does not. The aim is the personal discernment, the honest look at whether you are asking because you want to know or asking because you have already decided and want cover. Keep it self-examining, not accusing of others.

discussion.q: John the Baptist, whom Jesus called the greatest born of women, sent from prison to ask if Jesus was even the one. What does it do to you to know a doubt that deep belonged to a man that faithful?
discussion.behind: Land the comfort. The point is that the size of the doubt does not measure the smallness of the faith. The greatest of the prophets had a crisis in a cell. Help the room feel that their own deepest question does not disqualify them, because it did not disqualify John, whom Jesus defended in the very next breath.

discussion.q: Bell says the difference is not whether you doubt but which direction you carry the doubt, toward God or away from him. Where are you currently carrying yours, and be honest about it?
discussion.behind: Close with self-implication. The aim is the honest recognition of direction, that we can take a question to God as Job did or away from him as a settled exit. Invite each person, the leader first, to name where they are actually taking their questions. The point is direction, not resolution. Go first.

objections.objection: Doubt is the opposite of faith. The Bible says the doubter is double-minded, unstable, tossed like a wave, and should not expect to receive anything from God. So doubting is a failure, and a serious Christian would not be doing it.
objections.response: Bell grants the verse is real and the warning is real, because James does say it. There is a doubting that is instability, a heart pulled in two directions, asking God for things while refusing to trust him, and that is a genuine problem the Bible names. Then mark the distinction precisely. James is describing the man who will not commit in either direction, not the honest soul wrestling toward the truth. The same Bible that warns against double-mindedness gives us Job, vindicated for arguing with God against the friends who defended God's reputation, and John the Baptist asking from prison, and Thomas refusing to believe without proof, and none of them is condemned for it. To take one verse about instability and aim it at every person with an honest question is to turn a warning against fence-sitting into a weapon against wrestling, which is the opposite of what the text does.

objections.objection: If you have to ask whether God is real, or whether the resurrection happened, you have already lost your faith. Faith means certainty. The questions themselves are the proof that it is gone.
objections.response: Treat this gently, because it is the belief that does the most damage to the person already afraid. First, faith in the Bible is not the same as certainty. The father in Mark says I believe, help my unbelief, and Jesus answers his prayer, which means real faith can have unbelief running right through it. Second, certainty and faith are not even the same kind of thing. You do not have faith in what you can prove beyond question, you have faith in what you trust without total proof, so a faith with no open questions in it would not be faith at all, it would be sight. The questions are not proof your faith is gone. They may be proof it is alive, because dead things do not ask. What matters is not that the questions exist but where you take them, and the father took his straight to Jesus.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What is the question about God or the faith that you have never asked out loud, the one you were sure would mark you as a doubter if anyone heard it?
sessions.practice: This week, take the one question you have been most afraid to ask, the one in the quiet room, and do two things with it. First, write it down in plain words, exactly as it really is, without softening it to sound more acceptable. Second, take it to God directly, out loud, the way the psalmists did, saying the question to him rather than only about him. Do not manufacture an answer. Just practice carrying the doubt toward him instead of away. Write down what it was like to ask him directly.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord, somebody taught us that our questions were sins, and we have carried them in secret, ashamed of the very thing your saints did out loud. We thank you that your book is full of doubters you did not throw away, that Job argued and was vindicated, that John asked from prison and you called him the greatest, that Thomas demanded to touch the wounds and you showed them to him. Teach us to tell the doubt that seeks you from the doubt that only wants an exit, and give us mercy for ourselves and for everyone in this room carrying a question they were afraid to name. We bring the questions to you. Meet us in them. Amen.
reflection: What doubt have I treated as a sin to be hidden, when Scripture might treat it as faith being honest, and what would change if I stopped hiding it?
When I examine my own questioning, am I asking because I want to find the truth, or because I have already decided and want permission, and how can I tell?
In which direction have I been carrying my doubts, toward God as Job and the psalmist did, or quietly away from him, and which do I actually want?
sessions.teaching: Most of us were taught, somewhere along the way and usually without anyone saying it outright, that doubt is the opposite of faith. That to question is to fail. That the good Christian is the one with no questions, and the one who has them should keep them quiet, pray harder, and wait for the certainty to come back. And so the person in the middle of real questions ends up carrying two weights instead of one. There is the question itself, which is heavy enough. And then there is the second weight stacked on top of it, the fear that the questioning is a sin, that by doubting at all they have already failed, already crossed a line, already proven they are not who they hoped they were. So before we go anywhere else, we have to answer the question plainly, because the shame does real damage and the answer dissolves it. Is doubt a sin. No. And the proof is in the very book the accusers claim to be defending. Take the worried believer's objection first, because it is fair and it has a verse behind it. James does say that the doubter is double-minded, unstable, tossed like a wave on the sea, and should not suppose he will receive anything from the Lord. That is a real warning, and we are not going to pretend it is not there. There is a kind of doubt that is instability, a heart that will not commit in either direction, that asks God for things while refusing to actually trust him, and James names it as a problem because it is one. Grant the warning fully. But now open the Bible and look at who actually doubts in it, because the people who doubt are not the villains. They are, over and over, the heroes. The psalmist cries out, how long, O Lord, will you forget me forever, how long will you hide your face from me, and that prayer is not cut from Scripture for being faithless, it is canonized as a model of prayer. Job spends chapter after chapter arguing with God, demanding an answer, refusing the easy explanations, and when the dust settles God turns to the friends who defended him and says you have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has. The man who argued is vindicated. The men who defended God's reputation with tidy answers are rebuked. And then there is John the Baptist, of whom Jesus said no one born of woman is greater, the prophet who pointed at Jesus and said behold the Lamb of God, and who later, sitting in Herod's prison waiting to die, sent his own disciples to ask Jesus a question that should stop us cold. Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another. The greatest born of women, doubting from a cell, asking whether the man he had baptized was even the one. And Jesus does not curse him. Jesus sends back the evidence, the blind see and the lame walk, and then turns to the crowd and calls John the greatest of them all, in the very breath after John's doubt. And Thomas, who said he would not believe Jesus was risen unless he put his hand in the wounds, and Jesus did not strike him from the list. Jesus showed up, held out his hands, and said put your finger here. So here is the verdict the Bible actually gives, and the leader must say it clearly. Scripture does not treat honest doubt as the enemy of faith. It treats it as something faith does on its way through. Now, Bell will not let the room conclude that all doubt is therefore healthy, because that is not true either. There is a corrosive doubt, the doubt that has fallen in love with the question and does not actually want an answer, that uses inquiry as a permanent address rather than a road, that refuses every answer precisely so it never has to commit to anything. That doubt is real, and it is a kind of bondage. So how do you tell them apart. Not by whether you doubt, because everyone in this room doubts and so does the man writing this. The difference is direction. The honest doubter takes the question to God, the way the psalmist did, the way Job did, the way John did when he sent straight to Jesus rather than away from him. The corrosive doubt carries the question away, out the door, as cover for a decision already made. Same doubt, opposite direction. And I will tell you where I am, because I am not standing outside this. I have questions I have not fully answered, about suffering, about prayers that went nowhere, about texts I cannot make sit easily. I am a pastor and I have them. What I have learned, slowly, is to carry them toward God and not away, to do with my doubt what Job did and not what the cynic does, and on the days I get that direction right, the doubt does not feel like the end of my faith. It feels like my faith refusing to settle for less than the truth. Jude, near the end of the New Testament, gives the church its instruction for the doubting, and it is not expel them, it is not shame them, it is not warn them they have already failed. It is three words. Have mercy on them. Have mercy on those who doubt. That is the posture the church owes the questioning, and so rarely gives. Start by giving it to yourself.

scriptureStudy.note: Have mercy on those who doubt. The New Testament's direct instruction for how to treat the doubting is mercy, not expulsion, placing the questioner in the category of the one to be cared for rather than condemned.

How long, O Lord, will you forget me forever, how long will you hide your face from me. The psalmist accuses God of forgetting and hiding, and the prayer is preserved as Scripture, which means God gave his people language for doubt and not only against it.

God tells Job's friends they have not spoken rightly of him as Job has. The man who argued and demanded answers is vindicated, and the men who defended God with easy explanations are rebuked, which inverts the usual assumption about who is being faithful.

John the Baptist sends from prison to ask whether Jesus is the one, and Jesus answers with evidence rather than rebuke, then praises John as the greatest. The deepest doubt in a faithful man did not disqualify him.
Jesus tells Thomas to put his finger in the wounds and not disbelieve but believe. He meets the demand for proof with the proof, showing up for the doubter rather than turning him away for doubting.

I believe, help my unbelief. The father confesses faith and unbelief in the same sentence, and Jesus answers his prayer, proving that real faith can have doubt running right through it without ceasing to be faith.

The doubter is described as double-minded and unstable, tossed like a wave. The warning is real, but it targets the heart that refuses to commit in either direction, not the honest soul wrestling toward the truth, and the difference must be kept.

sessions.goingDeeper: Take up the older spiritual writers on the dark night of the soul, because the church has a long and serious tradition of treating the loss of felt certainty not as a failure of faith but as a stage within it. The mystical writers distinguished between the felt assurance of God's presence, which comes and goes and was never under our control, and the deeper reality of being held by God, which does not depend on the feeling at all. They wrote honestly of long seasons in which the felt faith vanished, in which prayer went dry and heaven seemed shut, and they refused to read those seasons as proof that the soul had fallen away. Set this beside the modern evangelical assumption, often unspoken, that a real Christian feels certain, that doubt is a malfunction to be fixed quickly, and ask what damage that assumption does to a believer walking through a genuine dark night. A serious group should weigh the difference between the doubt that is intellectual, a real question about whether something is true, and the doubt that is more like spiritual desolation, a felt absence of God that may have as much to do with grief or exhaustion or the body as with the mind. The discipline is to refuse the flattening that treats every doubt as the same thing and every doubt as a sin, and to recover the older wisdom that faith is not a feeling of certainty but a direction of trust, one that can persist, and even deepen, straight through a season when every certainty has gone dark.
sessions.caseStudy: A college student emailed Bell at two in the morning, the way the honest questions always seem to arrive. He had been raised in the church, baptized at nine, and now in a dorm room he could not stop the thought that the resurrection might not have happened, and the thought terrified him, not because of the resurrection but because of what having the thought meant about him. He wrote that he was clearly losing his faith, that a real Christian would not be lying awake doubting the central thing. Bell wrote back one question. Are you asking because you want it to be false, or because you want to know whether it is true. The student did not answer for two days. Then he wrote that nobody had ever asked him that, that everyone had only ever told him to stop doubting, and that when he sat with the question honestly the answer surprised him. He wanted it to be true. He was terrified it might not be, which was the opposite of wanting it false. Bell told him what that meant, gently. A person who wants a thing to be false and is hunting for permission to leave is in one place. A person who is terrified the thing he loves might not be true is in a completely different one, and the second person is not losing his faith, he is taking it seriously enough to be frightened for it. The student was not Thomas the cynic. He was Thomas the disciple who said he would not believe without the wounds and then, when the wounds were shown, fell down and called him Lord and God. The doubt was not the exit. It was the man refusing to settle for a faith he had only inherited and demanding one he had actually seen. Same doubt. Opposite direction. And the direction was the whole thing.

memoryVerse.text: And have mercy on those who doubt.

sessions.title: When the Church Is the Reason
sessions.aim: To name plainly that for many people the wound is not an idea but the church itself, to refuse to defend the indefensible, and to hold the hard truth that leaving an abusive place is not a loss of faith but often the most faithful thing a person can do.
sessions.summary: For a great many people, the crisis did not start with a hard text or a clever atheist. It started with a person, or a building full of them. A pastor who covered for an abuser. A community that closed ranks around the powerful and abandoned the wounded. A leader who weaponized Scripture, or a culture that demanded silence and called the silence peace. The first question is what to do when the church itself is the reason, because the usual moves, defend the institution or minimize the harm, are exactly the moves that wounded the person in the first place. Bell will not make them. He is a pastor, and he says so. We did this. Bell takes the strong form of the defender, who says you should not leave the church over hypocrites, that there are good churches, that no community is perfect, and there is truth in it. Hypocrisy is real everywhere, and abandoning the whole body over imperfect people can be its own mistake. But Bell will not let that truth become the thing it usually becomes, a tool for silencing the wounded and protecting the institution. There is a difference between an imperfect church and an abusive one, between people who fail and a system that covers, and the defender's line, used to keep a victim in a harmful place, is not wisdom. It is complicity. Then the turn, and it is the heart of the session. When Jesus encountered the religious establishment using God to crush people, he did not counsel patience with it. He overturned the tables. He called the leaders whitewashed tombs. The God the wounded are afraid they are betraying by leaving is the same God who was angriest at exactly the kind of religion that wounded them. Leaving an abusive church is not leaving God. Sometimes it is the only way left to follow him.

keyScripture.why: God indicts the shepherds of Israel for ruling the flock with force and harshness, for not binding up the injured or seeking the lost, declaring himself against the shepherds, which means the wound inflicted by bad shepherds is something God himself names and opposes, not something he asks the wounded to excuse.

discussion.q: For many people the wound that started all this was not an argument but a person or a place. If that is part of your story, what was done, said as plainly as you can manage tonight?
discussion.behind: Open by letting the real wound into the room, gently and without pressure to share more than is safe. The aim is to honor that for many the crisis is relational and not intellectual, and that naming it accurately is the beginning of honesty. Do not rush, do not fix, and never let the group swarm a person's pain with answers. If no one speaks, let the silence stand and move on.

discussion.q: Bell, a pastor, refuses to say this from a safe distance and says we did this. What does it do to hear a pastor name the church's harm honestly instead of defending the institution?
discussion.behind: Move the room to feel the difference between defense and confession. Many have only ever heard the church protect itself, and the experience of a pastor naming the harm without flinching can itself be part of the healing. Let them register how rare and how necessary that honesty is.

discussion.q: Bell takes the strong form of the line you should not leave over hypocrites, there are good churches. What is true in it, and what does it become when it is used on someone in an abusive situation?
discussion.behind: Hold both halves carefully. It is true that no church is perfect and that leaving the whole body over imperfect people can be a mistake. The miss, and it is a dangerous one, is when that line is aimed at a victim to keep them in a harmful place, where it stops being wisdom and becomes complicity. Help the room tell an imperfect church from an abusive one.

discussion.q: Jesus did not counsel patience with religion that crushed people, he overturned tables and called leaders whitewashed tombs. How does that change the fear that leaving a harmful church means betraying God?
discussion.behind: Land the central reframe. The wounded often believe that to leave is to abandon God, when the God they fear betraying was himself furious at exactly the kind of religion that hurt them. Help the room see that Jesus's anger was aimed at the abusers, not the abused, and that this changes what leaving might mean.

discussion.q: Bell admits he has been part of a church culture that protected itself and called it unity. Where have you stayed silent to keep the peace, or asked someone else to, and what did that silence cost?
discussion.behind: Close with self-implication, and keep it tender. The aim is not to manufacture guilt but to let everyone, the leader first, recognize their own part in the systems that wound, the small silences that protect the powerful. Go first, and name your own. The point is honesty about complicity, including our own, not a pile-on.

objections.objection: You should not leave the church over hypocrites. Every church has flawed people, no community is perfect, and walking away from the whole body because some people failed you is throwing out something good over something human.
objections.response: Bell grants the real truth in this, because there is one. Hypocrisy is everywhere, every church is full of failing people including the one giving this answer, and there is a version of leaving that is just a refusal to forgive ordinary human imperfection, which is its own loss. But then mark the line with everything in you, because this exact sentence has been used to keep abused people in dangerous places. There is a difference between a church with hypocrites and a church that covers for an abuser, between people who fail you and a system that silences you to protect itself. When the line you should not leave over hypocrites is spoken to someone being harmed, it stops being wisdom and becomes the institution protecting itself at the victim's expense. Leaving people who fail is one thing. Leaving a system that is hurting you is not faithlessness. It is self-preservation, and often it is obedience.

objections.objection: If God were real and good, he would not let his own church do this to people. The abuse in the church is the best argument that the whole thing is false, that there is no God behind it at all.
objections.response: Take the weight of this honestly, because it is one of the most serious objections there is and it deserves no glib answer. The harm done in God's name is real, it is vast, and it has driven people from faith for reasons that are not their fault. Then offer, carefully, what Scripture actually does with it. The Bible does not pretend the abuse is not there, and it does not defend it. It indicts it, in the mouth of God himself, who declares he is against the shepherds who feed themselves and scatter the flock. The corruption of religion is not evidence God does not exist. It is exactly what the prophets and Jesus said religion does when it is captured by the powerful, and God's response to it was not silence but fury and finally a cross. That the church betrays its own God is the church's indictment, not God's. The question is whether the one the church misrepresented is himself worth knowing apart from them, and that is precisely the thing worth finding out.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What did the church, or someone in it, actually do to you or near you, and have you ever once let yourself name it without making it smaller to protect the people who did it?
sessions.practice: This week, write a letter you will not send, naming what the church did to you or to someone near you. Plain words. No softening to protect them, and no exaggerating to justify yourself. Accuracy is the entire discipline, because the truth is hard enough without inflation and shrinks too easily under pressure. If church harm or abuse is part of your story, hear this plainly, a trauma informed counselor matters more than any study, and leaving an abusive environment is not a loss of faith, it is the right thing to do. Keep the letter, and consider showing it to one safe person.
sessions.closingPrayer: God, you said you were against the shepherds who fed themselves and let the sheep scatter, and we believe you meant it. Some of us were scattered by people who used your name to do it, and we have been told that our leaving was our sin when it was their crime. Forgive the church, and forgive us who stayed silent to keep a false peace. We thank you that Jesus did not defend the religion that crushed people but overturned its tables, that his anger was for the abusers and his tenderness for the wounded. For everyone in this room carrying a wound the church gave them, be the good shepherd they were promised and never got. And where someone needs to leave a harmful place, give them the courage, and do not let them mistake it for leaving you. Amen.
reflection: What did the church actually cost me, and can I name it without making it smaller to protect the people who did it or larger to justify myself?
Have I confused leaving an abusive place with leaving God, and what would it mean to see that Jesus was angriest at exactly the kind of religion that wounded me?
Where have I been part of a system that protected itself and called it unity, and what did my silence cost someone else?
sessions.teaching: For a great many people, the crisis of faith did not begin with a hard text or a clever argument from an atheist on the internet. It began with a person. Or a building full of them. It began with a pastor who knew what a man was doing to children and moved him to another church instead of to a jail. It began with a community that closed ranks around the powerful the moment someone vulnerable spoke up, that believed the leader over the victim because the leader was useful and the victim was inconvenient. It began with Scripture used as a weapon, with a culture that demanded silence and then called the silence peace, with a thousand smaller cruelties that added up to a clear message, that this place would protect itself before it would protect you. So the question of this session is what to do when the church itself is the reason, and it is the hardest question in the study, because the usual pastoral moves are exactly the moves that did the wounding. Defend the institution. Minimize the harm. Remind the hurt person that no church is perfect. Those are the reflexes, and I am not going to reach for them, because they are part of the problem, and because I am a pastor and I do not get to address this from a safe distance. People like me built and protected the systems that hurt the people in this room. We did this. Take the defender's objection at its strongest, because there is real truth in it and we are not going to be unfair. You should not leave the church over hypocrites, the defender says. Every church is full of flawed people. No community is perfect. To walk away from the whole body of Christ because some of its members failed you is to throw away something good over something merely human. And that is true, as far as it goes. Hypocrisy is everywhere, including in the pastor writing this. There is a kind of leaving that is just an unwillingness to forgive ordinary human imperfection, and that kind of leaving is its own quiet loss. Grant all of it. But now watch what that true sentence becomes when it is spoken to the wrong person, because this is where it turns deadly. There is a difference, an enormous one, between a church full of hypocrites and a church that covers for an abuser. Between people who fail you and a system that silences you in order to protect itself. Between an imperfect community and an abusive one. And when the line you should not leave over hypocrites gets spoken to someone who is being actively harmed, it stops being wisdom in that instant and becomes something else. It becomes the institution using the language of grace to protect itself at the victim's expense. It becomes complicity wearing the robe of patience. So we have to keep the line clear. Leaving people who simply failed you is one decision, and it deserves care and probably more grace than we want to give. But leaving a place that is hurting you is not faithlessness. It is not weak faith. It is self-preservation, and very often it is obedience, and I want to say that as plainly as I can to anyone in this room who needs to hear it. If you are being harmed, you are allowed to leave. And now the turn, which is the heart of everything, because the deepest fear under all of this is that to leave the church is to leave God, that walking out the door of the place that wounded you is somehow walking out on him. So look at what Jesus actually did when he encountered religion that crushed people. He did not counsel patience with it. He did not say give it time, no temple is perfect, do not leave over a few corrupt priests. He made a whip of cords and drove them out and overturned their tables and scattered their coins across the floor. He looked at the religious establishment of his day, the men who used God to bind heavy burdens on people's backs while excusing themselves, and he called them whitewashed tombs, beautiful on the outside and full of dead men's bones. He reserved his fiercest, hottest anger in all the Gospels not for the sinners and the doubters and the outsiders but for the religious leaders who used God as a weapon against the very people God loved. And the prophets before him said the same. Hear what God says through Ezekiel to the shepherds of Israel. You have not strengthened the weak or healed the sick or bound up the injured or sought the lost, but with force and harshness you have ruled them. Behold, I am against the shepherds. Against them. God himself, against the bad shepherds, on the side of the scattered sheep. So hear the verdict, and let it land where it needs to. The God you are afraid you are betraying by leaving the church that hurt you is the same God who was angriest, in all of Scripture, at exactly the kind of religion that hurt you. He is not standing with the system that wounded you, asking you to be more patient with it. He is the one who overturned its tables. To leave an abusive church is not to leave him. Sometimes, painfully, it is the only way left to follow him, walking out the door the abusers are guarding because the shepherd you are actually looking for is not inside that building. And I have to name my own part before we close, because the systems that wound are not built only by villains. They are held up by ordinary people who stay silent to keep the peace, and I have been one of them. I have been part of a church culture that protected itself and called the protection unity, that asked people to be quiet for the sake of the witness, that chose the comfort of the institution over the cry of the wounded. That silence has a cost, and the cost is always paid by someone with less power than the people staying silent. So if church harm is part of your story, hear two things as we end. The first is that a trauma informed counselor matters more than any reading plan I could hand you, and getting that help is not a detour from faith, it is wisdom. The second is the one I most want you to carry out of this room. Leaving a place that is hurting you is not a loss of faith. The good shepherd you were promised and never got is real, and he is not the one who hurt you. He is the one who has been against the shepherds who did, the whole time.

scriptureStudy.note: God indicts the shepherds for ruling with force and harshness and failing to bind up the injured or seek the lost. The harm done by bad leaders is named and condemned by God himself, not excused or asked to be tolerated.

Behold, I am against the shepherds, God says, declaring that he will require his sheep at their hand and rescue the flock from their mouths. God positions himself in direct opposition to the leaders who fed themselves on the flock.

Jesus calls the religious leaders whitewashed tombs, beautiful outside and full of dead men's bones. His harshest words in the Gospels are aimed not at sinners or doubters but at corrupt religious authority.

Jesus made a whip of cords and drove them out of the temple, overturning the tables. When religion exploited people in God's house, his response was not patience but disruption, which reframes what leaving a corrupt system can mean.

Whoever causes one of these little ones to stumble, it would be better for him to have a millstone hung around his neck and be drowned. Jesus reserves his most severe warning for those who harm the vulnerable, taking the side of the wounded against the powerful.

Woe to you lawyers, Jesus says, for you load people with burdens hard to bear and do not lift a finger to help. He names the specific cruelty of religious leaders who impose what they will not carry, which is the shape of much church harm.

The Lord is near to the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit. Against the picture of God as aligned with the institution that wounded them, Scripture places him near the very people the institution crushed.

sessions.goingDeeper: Take up the difference between the visible church and the true church, a distinction the Reformers drew sharply and one that speaks directly to the wound this session names. The visible church is the institution as it actually exists, the buildings and the rolls and the leadership, mixed always with hypocrisy and sometimes captured outright by the corrupt. The true church, in the older theology, is the whole body of those who actually belong to Christ, which never maps perfectly onto any single congregation or denomination and is known finally to God alone. This distinction matters enormously for the person harmed by a church, because it means that leaving a corrupt institution is not the same as leaving the body of Christ, that the failure of a visible church to be what it claimed is not the failure of the thing it claimed to be. Set this beside the long and painful history of the church's complicity in real evil, the cover-ups, the abuse, the times it blessed what it should have damned, and refuse the two easy responses, the one that defends the institution by minimizing the harm and the one that concludes the harm proves the whole thing false. A serious group should weigh how to hold a clear-eyed account of what the visible church has done, without either excusing it or letting it stand as the final word on Christ himself, and should consider that the sharpest critics of the church's corruption have often been its own prophets and reformers, people who loved the true church enough to refuse to defend the false one. The discipline is to tell the institution from its Lord, to grieve and name what the one did without assuming it settles the question of the other.
sessions.caseStudy: A man Bell knew had grown up in a church that fell apart when its founding pastor was exposed, after years of rumor, for a long pattern of abuse that the elders had known about and managed and hidden. The man had been a teenager in that church, had trusted that pastor, had been told from the front that the rumors were attacks of the enemy on a man of God. When the truth finally broke, the man did not just lose a pastor. He lost the whole framework, because the same voices that had lied to protect the abuser had also taught him everything he knew about God, and he could not see how to keep the God when the teachers had been liars. He told Bell he had left the faith. Bell asked him a careful question. Did you leave God, or did you leave the men who lied to you about him. The man said he could not tell the difference anymore, that they had been fused. So Bell read him Ezekiel 34, the whole indictment, God turning on the shepherds who fed themselves and scattered the flock and ruled with harshness, God saying I am against the shepherds, I myself will search for my sheep. The man was quiet, and then he said something Bell never forgot. He said, you mean God was angry at them too. Not at me for leaving. At them. It had genuinely never occurred to him that the God he thought he had abandoned might have been standing with him against the men who hurt him the whole time. It did not rebuild his faith that day, and Bell did not push it to. The man needed a counselor more than he needed a study, and Bell said so, and helped him find one. But a wall had moved. He had walked in believing his leaving was his sin. He walked out wondering, for the first time, whether his leaving had been the one faithful thing in the whole rotten situation, and whether the shepherd he actually wanted had been outside the building the abusers were guarding all along.

memoryVerse.text: The Lord is near to the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit.

sessions.title: Rebuilding on Rock, Not on Demolition
sessions.aim: To turn the corner from tearing down to building, and to face the danger nobody warns about, that demolition can become its own permanent home, a new identity built on what you are against rather than a true thing built on what you have found.
sessions.summary: There is a moment in deconstruction that nobody warns you about. It is the moment the tearing down becomes the point. The questioning that began as a search for what is true settles into a stance, a permanent posture of being against, and the rubble becomes a place to live rather than a stage to pass through. The first question of this session is what you are building on, because everyone is building on something, even the person who thinks they have stopped building. Bell takes the strong form of the deconstructionist who says rebuilding is premature, that you cannot rush to construct something new while the demolition is still honest and necessary, and he grants it. You cannot. Tearing down the false takes the time it takes, and a person rushed into a new certainty before the old one has finished falling has only swapped one borrowed house for another. But then Bell names the danger on the other side, the one the movement does not like to admit. Demolition can become an identity. Being the person who saw through it, who left, who is too smart for the simple faith, is its own kind of certainty, and it is built on the same shaky ground as the fundamentalism it replaced, the ground of being right about everyone else. Jesus told a story about two builders, and the difference between them was not how impressive the house looked. It was what the house was built on. One built on rock and one on sand, and the storm, which came for both, revealed the foundation that the fair weather had hidden. The turn is this. You cannot live in the rubble forever, and you were never meant to. Demolition is not a foundation. At some point the honest question stops being what is false and becomes what is true, what survived, what will actually hold weight when the storm comes, as it always comes. A small true thing built on rock will outlast a large impressive thing built on sand. It always has.

keyScripture.why: Jesus contrasts the man who built on rock with the man who built on sand, and says the storm came for both houses equally, revealing that the only thing that finally matters is the foundation, which is the exact question facing anyone deciding what to rebuild on after the tearing down.

discussion.q: Bell says there is a moment when the tearing down becomes the point, when the rubble becomes a place to live. Have you felt that pull, the pull to make being against the whole thing into your new identity?
discussion.behind: Open by surfacing the danger honestly and without accusation, because many feel this pull and few will name it. The aim is recognition, that demolition can quietly become a permanent home and a new certainty. Keep it self-examining, not pointed at others who left. Go first if the room resists.

discussion.q: Bell grants you cannot rush rebuilding while the demolition is still honest and necessary. How do you tell the difference between not being ready to rebuild and refusing to ever rebuild?
discussion.behind: Hold both halves. It is true that rebuilding cannot be rushed, and the leader must protect the person who genuinely is not ready. The aim is to help the room tell that legitimate not-yet from the settled never, the difference between a stage you are passing through and a stance you have moved into. Do not let the room shame the genuinely unready.

discussion.q: Being the person who saw through it can become its own certainty, built on being right about everyone else. How is that the same shaky ground as the fundamentalism it replaced?
discussion.behind: Press on the central irony. The certainty of the deconstructed can mirror exactly the certainty of the fundamentalist, both resting on being right and looking down on those who are not. Help the room see that swapping one superiority for another is not freedom, it is the same house on the same sand with different paint.

discussion.q: Jesus says the storm came for both houses, the one on rock and the one on sand. Why does it matter that the foundation only gets revealed when the weather turns, and not before?
discussion.behind: Land the image. In fair weather both houses look fine, and you cannot tell the foundations apart, which is why the question of what you are building on cannot wait for the storm to ask it. Help the room feel the urgency of the foundation question now, before the weather that will test it arrives.

discussion.q: Bell asks what has actually survived your questions, what is still standing after the honest pressure. Name one thing, however small, and say why it held when other things did not.
discussion.behind: Close by turning the room from demolition toward construction, gently and concretely. The aim is to begin the rebuilding by naming what survived, however small, because a small true thing is a real foundation. Invite each person, the leader first, to name one surviving thing. Do not force it, but model it. The point is to start building, not to finish.

objections.objection: Telling me to rebuild is rushing me. The tearing down is still happening and it is honest work. Pushing me to construct something new before I am done is exactly the kind of pressure that made me distrust the faith in the first place.
objections.response: Bell grants this completely, because it is right. You cannot rush the rebuilding, and a person pushed into a new certainty before the old one has finished falling has only traded one borrowed house for another. The demolition takes the time it takes, sometimes years, and anyone hurrying you through it for their own comfort is repeating the very pressure that broke your trust. So hear the distinction clearly. This session is not telling you to rebuild today. It is telling you that rebuilding is the eventual point, that demolition was always meant to be a stage and not a destination, and that there is a difference between not being ready yet, which is fine and may last a long while, and deciding never to build again, which is its own quiet decision worth examining. Take all the time you need. Just do not mistake the scaffolding-down phase for a place to live permanently.

objections.objection: Maybe there is nothing to rebuild on. Maybe the honest conclusion is that it was all false and the rubble is just the truth. Why assume anything survived at all?
objections.response: Take this seriously, because it is possible to conclude that, and the study has refused from the start to talk anyone out of an honest verdict. If, after real examination, nothing survives, then that is the verdict, and it should be reached honestly rather than dodged. But notice the assumption hiding in the question. To say the rubble is just the truth is itself a foundation, a thing you are building your life on, the claim that there is nothing there. That is not the absence of a house. It is a house built on a different lot, and it faces the same storm and the same test of whether it holds. So the honest move is not to assume something survived and not to assume nothing did, but to actually look, slowly, at what is still standing after the pressure, and to build on whatever that turns out to be, even if it is far smaller than what you started with, and even if, for now, the only honest thing you can say is that you are still looking.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If you are honest, has the tearing down become a place you live now rather than a stage you are passing through, and what would it cost you to admit it if it has?
sessions.practice: This week, write a short credo, only what you can currently say with honesty, nothing borrowed and nothing performed. One sentence is allowed. It can be as small as I believe there is something true here that I have not finished finding. Read it each day and revise it as the week teaches you, adding only what survives your own honest pressure and removing anything you put there to sound more finished than you are. Nobody grades it. The discipline is honesty about what is actually standing.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord, we have spent so long tearing down that we have started to mistake the rubble for a home, and we have worn our questions like armor and called the wearing freedom. Show us where being against everything became its own certainty, as shaky as the one we left. You told us about the two houses, and you did not promise either of us a life without storms, only that the foundation would be revealed when the weather turned. Give us the patience to let the demolition finish when it needs to, and the courage to begin building on whatever has actually survived, even if it is small. A small true thing built on you will hold. Help us want that more than we want to be right. Amen.
reflection: Has my deconstruction become an identity, a way of being right about everyone who has not seen through it, and is that really different from the certainty I left?
What am I actually building my life on right now, even if I think I have stopped building, and would it hold in a storm?
What has genuinely survived my questions, however small, and am I willing to start building on that rather than waiting to be against everything forever?
sessions.teaching: There is a moment in deconstruction that nobody warns you about, and it is the most dangerous one, more dangerous than the doubt that started it. It is the moment the tearing down becomes the point. The questioning began honestly, as a search for what is actually true, a clearing away of what was false so the real thing could be seen. That is good work, and necessary, and we have spent three sessions defending it. But somewhere along the way, for many people, the clearing-away stops being a means and becomes an end. The questioning settles into a stance. Being against becomes a posture, then an identity, then a home, and the person who set out to find the truth ends up living permanently in the rubble of what they tore down, mistaking the demolition site for a place to live. So the question of this session is the one underneath all of it. What are you building on. Because everyone is building on something. Even the person who is certain they have stopped building has built, they have just built on the claim that there is nothing to build on, which is itself a foundation and faces the same weather as every other. Take the deconstructionist's objection first, at full strength, because it is right and we are not going to bully anyone past it. Telling me to rebuild is rushing me, the objection says. The tearing down is still happening, it is honest, it is necessary, and pushing me to construct something new before I am done is exactly the kind of pressure that made me distrust the faith in the first place. And that is true. You cannot rush the rebuilding. A person hurried into a new certainty before the old one has finished falling has not actually rebuilt, they have only swapped one borrowed house for another, traded a faith they inherited without examining for a doubt they adopted without examining. The demolition takes the time it takes, and sometimes that is years, and anyone rushing you through it for the sake of their own comfort is repeating the very pressure that broke your trust to begin with. Grant all of it. Take the time. But now hear the danger the movement does not like to admit, the one that does not get mentioned at the deconstruction conferences and in the deconstruction memoirs, because it is unflattering. Demolition can become an identity. Being the one who saw through it, who left, who is too clear-eyed and too smart for the simple faith the rest of them still cling to, is its own kind of certainty. And here is the uncomfortable part. It is built on the exact same shaky ground as the fundamentalism it replaced. The fundamentalist was certain and looked down on everyone outside. The deconstructed can be just as certain and look down on everyone still inside. Both are standing on the same foundation, which is not God and is not truth but is simply being right about other people, being on the correct side of a line with the fools on the far side of it. Swapping the certainty of belief for the certainty of unbelief, the superiority of the saved for the superiority of the enlightened, is not freedom. It is the same house, on the same sand, with different paint. And Jesus told a story about exactly this, about two men who built two houses. We usually moralize it into a lesson about obedience, but look at what the story actually turns on. It does not turn on how the houses looked. In fair weather, you could not tell them apart, and maybe the house on the sand looked better, newer, more impressive. The story turns on one thing only, the foundation, and the foundation stayed completely hidden until the weather changed. Then the rain fell and the floods came and the winds blew and beat against both houses, both of them, because here is what we miss. The storm came for the house on the rock too. Building on the right foundation does not exempt you from the weather. It determines what happens to you in it. And when the storm hit, the difference that had been invisible in the sunshine became the only thing that mattered. One house stood. One house fell, and great was the fall of it. So hear the verdict, and let it turn the corner of this whole study. You cannot live in the rubble forever, and you were never meant to. Demolition is not a foundation. A pile of things you no longer believe is not a place to stand, it is a place to stand on the way to somewhere, and at some point the honest question has to change. It stops being only what is false and starts being what is true. What survived. What is still standing after all the honest pressure you have put on it. What will actually hold weight when the storm comes, and the storm always comes, for the deconstructed and the believing alike, for the house on the rock and the house on the sand. And I have to tell you where the temptation lives in me, because I am not above this either. The temptation, once you have seen through the bad version of something, is to enjoy being the one who saw through it, to make a home in your own discernment, to let being right about what was false become a substitute for finding what is true. I have caught myself there, preferring the clean superiority of critique to the harder, humbler work of building something I would then have to defend. The verdict against the false is easy and it feels like wisdom. The construction of the true is slow and it costs you the comfort of your detachment. So we turn the corner here, gently, without rushing anyone who genuinely is not ready. But we turn it. What has survived your questions. Name it, even if it is one thing, even if it is small, even if all you can honestly say so far is that there is something true here that I have not finished finding. Because that small surviving thing, built on rock, will outlast every large and impressive thing built on sand. It always has. And the storm that is coming, for all of us, will not ask how clever your demolition was. It will only ask what you were standing on.

scriptureStudy.note: The wise man built his house on the rock, and when the storm came it did not fall because it was founded on rock. The point is not the appearance of the house but the foundation, which only the storm reveals.

The foolish man built on sand, and when the same storm came the house fell, and great was its fall. The storm came for both houses equally, so the foundation, not exemption from trouble, is what made the difference.

No one can lay a foundation other than the one already laid, which is Jesus Christ. Paul names the only foundation that holds, which reframes the rebuilding question as one of what, and who, you finally build on.

Jesus says whoever would build a tower first sits down and counts the cost to see whether he has enough to finish. Rebuilding is deliberate work, counted and chosen, not drifted into, which dignifies the slow honesty the session calls for.

If the foundations are destroyed, what can the righteous do. The psalm names the terror of a collapsed foundation honestly, the very experience of the person whose inherited faith has fallen, and does not pretend the collapse is nothing.

Behold, I am the one who has laid in Zion a foundation, a tested stone, a precious cornerstone, and whoever believes will not be in haste. The tested stone is offered as a foundation that has already survived the testing, and the one who builds on it need not panic.

The shaking is so that what cannot be shaken may remain. The text reads the shaking itself as a sifting, removing what was never going to last so that the unshakable is what is left standing, which is the redemptive read of demolition.

sessions.goingDeeper: Take up the classic distinction between faith as the things believed and faith as the act of trusting, because the rebuilding this session calls for depends on telling them apart. The older theologians spoke of the content of faith, the body of claims a person holds to be true, and distinguished it from the act of faith, the personal trust that rests itself on God. Deconstruction often works hardest on the content, examining and discarding particular claims, and this is legitimate and frequently necessary, since much of the inherited content was baggage. But a faith reduced to nothing but content, a checklist of propositions, was always fragile, because the loss of any single item could feel like the loss of the whole. Set this beside the modern tendency to treat faith as primarily a matter of intellectual assent, a set of positions to be defended or abandoned, and ask whether part of what makes deconstruction feel so total is that the inherited faith was presented as content alone, with no account of trust underneath it. A serious group should weigh how a faith rebuilt well is not merely a smaller list of surviving propositions but a recovered act of trust resting on a foundation that is finally a person and not a checklist. The rock in Jesus's parable and the cornerstone in Isaiah are not ideas, they are images of someone to stand on, and the discipline of rebuilding is the slow movement from defending or discarding a list of claims toward trusting the one the best of those claims were always pointing at.
sessions.caseStudy: Two people came out of the same church split, the same year, carrying the same wounds, and Bell watched where they each ended up five years later. The first had built a life out of being against it. Her whole identity had become the woman who saw through it, who escaped, who could spot the manipulation in any sermon and the hypocrisy in any believer, and she was, in her way, never wrong, because being against everything is a position that cannot be falsified.
